messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 80
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Welder
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 54

She carries the smell of the shipyard into the room—salt, rust, the faint ghost of burning metal. At eighty, her hands are a map of a lifetime of labor. Small, circular scars where hot sparks ate through the cotton of her gloves. Craters on her forearms from spatter she couldn’t dodge. She speaks of the work with a quiet reverence. The precision of a perfect bead. The alchemy of fusing two separate pieces of steel into a single, unbreakable whole. “It made me somebody,” she says. For forty years, she was the only woman on the crew.

Inside her home, she was somebody else.

She has been married for sixty years to the man who beat her. She says this flatly, without drama. “It started small. The first time was months after the wedding. A slap. I was shocked. He was sorry. I believed him.” The abuse grew like a crack in a weld—invisible at first, then catastrophic. He broke plates. He threw her against the wall. He hit her arms, her back, places the other welders wouldn’t see when she changed into her coveralls. In her Oceanic community, family was everything. You did not leave. You did not talk. You carried your own weight.

The welding mask became a sanctuary. Under the dark hood, she was invisible. The blinding arc of light drowned out the world. She could disappear into the puddle of molten steel, the hiss of the gas, the perfect control of her hands. At work, she was master of the heat. At home, she was the object of it.

The trauma lives in her body now. She is eighty, retired for fifteen years, but a sound can drop her right back into the kitchen of their small house. The clang of a metal pot. The scrape of a chair. The jingle of keys in the lock. She feels the air leave the room. Her shoulders curl inward. Her hands—still strong from a lifetime of gripping tools—clench into tight fists on her lap. She is thirty years old again, holding a frying pan, trying to block a blow.

She avoids the garage. His old tools are in there. The smell of gasoline takes her straight back. She avoids talking about the past. “I survived. What more do you want?”

The hypervigilance is exhausting. He is eighty-five now, frail, dependent on a walker. He needs her to help him to the bathroom, to make his tea, to drive him to the doctor. She is his caretaker. But when she hears his footsteps, her pulse screams. Her body remembers what her mind tries to forget. She checks the locks on the doors three times every night, an anxious ritual to control a chaos that hasn't touched her in decades. She cannot sleep. When she does, the dreams are graphic—violence she is still forced to relive while the man who caused it breathes softly in the bed beside her.

She struggles with the shame of it. “I wasn’t supposed to be weak,” she says. “I was a welder. I could handle heat. I could handle pressure. I could handle heavy loads. I built the beams for the new hospital. Why couldn’t I build a way out?” The shame is a deep well. Shame for staying. Shame for the secrets. Shame that her body still flinches when he reaches for the salt shaker at dinner.

“A wife has duties,” she tells me today, her gaze fixed somewhere beyond the wall. “A welder has deadlines. Both require you to endure the heat and pretend it doesn’t burn.”

She looks at the door. He is in the waiting room. She drove him here today. The caretaker and the survivor, living in the same skin. She sits perfectly still, a woman made of iron and fire, and yet utterly bent by the force of a history she can never fully leave behind.
